sources.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
sources.description:
PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope

Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

sources.title: EU wants ‘closest possible relationship’ with UK after agreeing Brexit reset deal – live
sources.description:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK

Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

“Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single biggest growth intervention in this Parliament.”

sources.title: Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit
sources.description:
Agreements reached on food and drink, emissions and to allow young people to move around continent, but may be derailed over student fees

Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides.

At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

sources.title: UK, EU seek closer ties a decade after Brexit as Burnham visits Brussels
sources.description:
A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.
Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with UK government ministers and European commissioners.
Burnham has described the rare EU-UK summit - only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world's biggest trading bloc - as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained," he said this week.
Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc.
